newsitem.title: MEXICO: Texas, Mexico link up to battle money laundering.
newsitem.headline: Texas, Mexico link up to battle money laundering.

text.p: Mexico and Texas are uniting forces to combat money laundering along their 1,200-mile (1,900-km) border, Texas Attorney General Dan Morales said on Monday.

Morales said that by taking the unusual step of meeting with an individual U.S. state on Monday, Mexican Attorney General Antonio Lozano Gracia and anti-drug Commissioner Francisco Molina Ruiz demonstrated Mexico's resolve in battling drug trafficking.

"I think that Commissioner Molina recognises the necessity for attacking the problem of money laundering on all fronts," Morales said. "And I also think Commissioner Molina recognises the strategic importance of the state of Texas."
Money laundering is the system by which drug traffickers use banks and dummy corporations to account falsely for their income, which usually arrives in huge bundles of cash.
Morales said approximately $30 billion is laundered in the Texas-Mexico border region each year while the United States and Mexico together generate about $150 billion in money laundering annually.

One goal of Monday's meeting was to establish a method for direct cooperation between the Texas Office of the Attorney General and Mexico's National Drug Enforcement Institute headed by Molina, Morales said.
"The drug traffickers absolutely need the launderers," Morales said. "The launderers don't recognise borders. That's why we need to build and establish international responses."
Morales also said he would attempt to soothe frictions between the United States and Mexico that developed in April when top U.S. anti-drug officials were in Mexico for a three-day conference.

U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency chief Thomas Constantine said then that Mexican banks were laundering billions of dollars and planes loaded with cocaine were landing in Mexico only to leave reloaded with cash.
Mexico angrily rejected the charges, calling them "offensive."

"In the past there has been a tendency on the part of the United States to attempt to blame Mexico for this problem," Morales said. "I believe there is plenty of blame to go around on our side of the border. I regret that there have been unfortunate statements made in the past."
